$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$ 
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $det(A)=0$
- **II.** $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b$
- **III.** ${A}^{-1}$ does **not** exist" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is true by the second part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false. According to the first part of the invertible matrix theorem, the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ must exist.

Finally, only statement II is true."} {:db/id 17592186115884 :question/id #uuid "07b54935-f6c1-5cc5-a220-23bab58f39a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-47653" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{bmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},$ where $k$ is a constant such that $k\ne -1.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $det(A)\ne 0$

- **II.** $Ax=0$ has no solutions

- **III.** The lines $6x+2y=1$ and $-3x+ky=-2$ intersect at infinitely many points" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{bmatrix} \\  & =6\cdot k-2\cdot (-3) \\  & =6k+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $6k+6\ne 0$ if $k\ne -1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement III is false. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statement I is true."} {:db/id 17592186262854 :question/id #uuid "364a18ef-2de8-57d7-9e2f-631eb4651446" :question/math-academy-id "q-127931"} {:db/id 17592186262856 :question/id #uuid *If the lines intersect at one point, then $\text{__________}\,.$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

According to the invertible matrix theorem, if the lines $-x+y=1$ and $x+ky=1$ intersect at one point, then 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}
$$

is invertible and $det(A)\ne 0.$ 
Additionally, the unique solution to $Ax=0$ is $⟨0,0⟩$ and

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

has exactly one solution, which is the intersection point of the lines.

Therefore, the true statement is as follows:

*If the lines intersect at one point, then $\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ has 
 the unique solution $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$*"} {:db/id 17592186329822 :question/id #uuid "ffbb2a4c-595d-59cc-bffd-a39a18b105b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-47657"} {:db/id "b252a44d-8417-5bdc-8a9b-ad6e81276b7c" :question/math-academy-id "q-36075" :question/problem "Let 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.$
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $det(A)=0$
- **II.** $Ax=0$ has the unique  solution $⟨0,0⟩$
- **III.** $⟨5,-4⟩$ is a solution to $Ax=0$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 0 \\  & =-6\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is true by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false. Again,  according to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

Therefore, only statement II is true."} :step/id #uuid "028bab25-3fed-5252-aa96-72f7de3058fa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495203}} {:db/id 17592186495203 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495058 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3dac26d2-ebbe-5a1e-83fa-4b3b6d5b4e28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186494448} {:answer/id #uuid "551b68dd-eb85-5e01-8e30-fd3cc7694f1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186494491} {:answer/id #uuid "939de576-f6fe-534e-bcc7-b91eb70d6b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186494656} {:answer/id #uuid "c357f7bd-3a09-51e9-abea-8dc1deeb12c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186494778} {:answer/id #uuid "efaad133-59c6-5b2b-9d22-976c341550bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II  only" :db/id 17592186494886}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494448} :answer-field/id #uuid "273b6a9c-3dfc-5014-9117-506724cb00ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494934}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "11aeb2f0-20f1-51d5-8c52-39a1558cd757" :question/math-academy-id "q-47651" :question/problem "Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

*If the lines $y-x=1$ and $x+ky=4$, where $k$ is a constant, intersect at exactly one point, then $\text{__________}$ .*

I. the lines $y-x=0$ and $x+ky=0$ don't intersect

II. the lines $y-x=0$ and $x+ky=0$ intersect at infinitely many points

III. $det\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\ne 0$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that given $A=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

Notice that if we set 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

  

then the fourth part of the theorem is true. Hence,  all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem, only option III give us a true statement: 

- *If the lines $y-x=1$ and $x+ky=4$, where $k$ is a constant, intersect at exactly one point, then $det\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix}\ne 0$ .* $\,✓$"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-128139" :question/problem "Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

*If a $2\times 2$-matrix $A$ is invertible, then $\text{__________}$ . *

I. $det(A)\ne 0$
II. $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution
III. $Ax=0$ has infinitely many solutions

$$

- Statement I is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is true by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false since, according to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

"Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & k\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. 

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is true by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false since, according to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- **II.** The lines $2x+2y=2$ and $3x+ky=0$ intersect at infinitely many points

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 3 & k\end{bmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot k-3\cdot 2 \\  & =2k-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $2k-6\ne 0$ if $k\ne 3.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

- Statement III is true by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

-2\sqrt[4]{1-2x}+1$?" :question/worked-solution "The range of $\sqrt[4] x$ is

$$
\sqrt[4] x \ge 0
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[4]{1-2x} \ge 0
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-2$ and then adding $1$, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[4]{1 - 2x} & \ge 0 \\ -2\sqrt[4]{1 - 2x} & \le 0 \\ -2\sqrt[4]{1 - 2x} + 1 & \le 1 \\ f(x) & \le 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x) \in (-\infty,1]$.

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

$$
f(x)=\sqrt[n]{x}
$$

depends on whether the index $n$ of the radical is even or odd.

Let's start with the odd case first. What is the range of

$$
f(x) = -2\sqrt[3]{3x-2}+2
$$

First, recall that the range of

$$
y = \sqrt[3] x
$$

is
$y \in (-\infty,\infty)$.

Transformations do not change this interval. Therefore, the range of $f(x)$ is $y \in (-\infty,\infty)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "6b9dccc8-5bda-5458-a62d-5d74d82eb634" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4863 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "70a49b8b-925c-5999-90d0-2b2d817e962c" :step/math-academy-id 30458 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180410}} {:db/id 17592186180407 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179684 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179543 :question/id #uuid "7096f867-7d37-5630-a885-d0a4f4a6acb7" :question/math-academy-id "e-8142"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "52e02202-ebdf-5987-bbaf-b5eb204c3892" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049986} {:db/id 17592186050642}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180300} {:db/id 17592186180303}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Range of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index"} :step/id #uuid "d6b1dfbb-7d27-561e-82ff-dafcb19e06f5" :step/math-academy-id 30459} {:db/id 17592186180410 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179687 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179546 :question/id #uuid "9af3bd0c-c209-508f-b806-bb9426f2c0da" :question/math-academy-id "e-8719"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3abc2f98-9bbd-5a33-87fc-f9459fb18c60" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049528}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180301} {:db/id 17592186180302}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Range of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index"} :step/id #uuid "f116d4fa-4115-5e01-a07f-ef9053e45179" :step/math-academy-id 32415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180413}} {:db/id 17592186180413 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180686 :tutorial/content "Let's now focus on the even case. What is the range of

$$
g(x) = -3\sqrt[4]{2x-1}-2
$$

The range of $\sqrt[4] x$ is

$$
\sqrt[4] x \ge 0
$$

Now, let's apply transformations to the inequality above to turn the left-hand side into $g(x)$.

First, remember that horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[4]{2x-1} \ge 0
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-3$ and then subtracting $2$, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[4]{2x - 1} & \ge 0 \\ -3\sqrt[4]{2x - 1} & \le 0 \\ -3\sqrt[4]{2x - 1} - 2 & \le - 2 \\ g(x) & \le - 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $g(x) \in (-\infty,-2]$.

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is shown below.

:question/problem "Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[0,2]\times {-1,0,1}$ in the Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[0,2]\times {-1,0,1}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1,0,$ or $1.$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in [0,2],\,y\in {-1,0,1}}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}={(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [0,2]}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/de/de9bd6dc79cabf8230b0cec26233958aa0fbb001875b9942cbb7f4d36e6b08fb.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $0.$

$$
{S}_{2}={(x,0)\,:\,x\in [0,2]}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/81/819c31e4d29dbd3e18c7dea8df495a565d2ede866ec019c764704d6dc47f5c70.png)

Now, consider ${S}_{3}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,2]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{3}={(x,1)\,:\,x\in [0,2]}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/3f/3f335df98dc9cb33ccc96f87d24efa3bd78a4d4c271d0fbaf7ae5e8c30916d9e.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the three line segments shown below.

:question/problem "Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=Z\times R$ in the Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/3f/3fdfed680e3fb46adbe8a70aac86682aacb85d43e0675923f87658635fc89a1e.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/7f/7fbda500ecca7e18c9db9939ad78d4dcc6bf488bc7fc4de1137e764ce21a0254.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times R$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

"The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in [0,1]\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}=\{(0,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/1c/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}=\{(i,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,1],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](images/49/494c9d77b0ff339b90792270c9d641054a03a2918e3c56a93747b42a77ee3ccf.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,1]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

$$

$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,0.5]\times [0,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,0.5],b\in [0,1]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0.5,0),$ $(0.5,1),$ and $(0,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 4387} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199560 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $A$ and $B$ are sets, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](images/e7/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c18e6618-573b-5560-8d95-58ed56f05155" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c7652427-e5ff-5d02-9f23-39039f090aff" :step/math-academy-id 153383 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199078}} {:db/id 17592186199078 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198272 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198169 :question/id #uuid "bb40c174-3739-50df-835e-5d47c9902d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-13192"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c3a2b291-c6dd-58c8-a10f-d851511d7bfc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048899} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186050432} {:db/id 17592186050763} {:db/id 17592186050923}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198802} {:db/id 17592186198807} {:db/id 17592186287775} {:db/id 17592186287870} {:db/id 17592186287871} {:db/id 17592186389895} {:db/id 17592186390326} {:db/id 17592186421830} {:db/id 17592186422996} {:db/id 17592186561008} {:db/id 17592186561022}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "2190f1df-5853-5d8c-85e2-33f40f1f0f24" :step/math-academy-id 153384 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199079}} {:db/id 17592186199079 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199579 :tutorial/content "Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane!

$$

:question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/3e/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](images/0f/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/58/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](images/f0/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $[0,2]\times \{0\}:$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/3f/3fdfed680e3fb46adbe8a70aac86682aacb85d43e0675923f87658635fc89a1e.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/7f/7fbda500ecca7e18c9db9939ad78d4dcc6bf488bc7fc4de1137e764ce21a0254.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

is a representation of the set $S=R\times Z$ in the Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times Z
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in Z\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1.$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/8e/8e677c814756c4818c25da450d789c974787df60cf4bb18017a96593d3ecc180.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f9/f99beeb00c070048ee4ee7c1b6c9e077d7d4e0f3fd9e63aa12b5b58588e14dbb.png)

We can create the subsets $…{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times Z & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times Z$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by

$$
\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}
$$

This gives

$$
\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac {180^\circ} {\pi}\right) = 288^\circ
$$

Therefore

$$
\dfrac{8\pi}{5}
$$

is equivalent to $288^\circ$, which lies in the $4$th quadrant.

![](images/4c/4c60c3aecabe8f625d09843ae5bdbc1e7e5525c1f0e6ab894387320c5420cab8.png)

To express

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right)
$$

in terms of $\sin\theta_R$, we follow three steps:

1. Find its reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the function for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = \dfrac{8\pi}{5}
$$

is in the $4$th quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= 2π - θ \\
&= 2π - \frac{8π}{5} \\
&= \frac{10π}{5} - \frac{8π}{5} \\
&= \frac{2π}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right)
$$

, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\sin\theta_R = \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right)
$$

must be *negative* because the sine ratio is *always* negative in the $4$th quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right) = -\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050053} {:db/id 17592186050795} {:db/id 17592186051043} {:db/id 17592186193144 :question/id #uuid "12eccebd-490c-53ba-aead-ee1cd1b26f1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-156137"} {:db/id 17592186193388 :question/id #uuid "8bb99b4e-5f44-5929-ac69-41b61486bf9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-84524"} {:db/id 17592186192750 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192469 :question/id #uuid "0a1428c6-96e8-5c82-82b2-ed51375454ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-10829"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a7d5897-3360-59fb-9f64-2f9f641290be" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193145 :question/id #uuid "591a29eb-2bcd-5cc9-a169-2c2e3c38685b" :question/math-academy-id "q-156230"} {:db/id 17592186193373 :question/id #uuid "7c10b38f-e0b5-5dcf-88f0-5db1e7d6bda3" :question/math-academy-id "q-64638"}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Cosine of an Angle in Terms of a Reference Angle"} {:db/id 17592186192469 :question/id #uuid "0a1428c6-96e8-5c82-82b2-ed51375454ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-10829" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192750 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a7d5897-3360-59fb-9f64-2f9f641290be" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Cosine of an Angle in Terms of a Reference Angle"}] :question/problem "Express $\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{5}\right)$ in terms of a reference angle." :question/worked-solution "To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees.

θ_{R} &= π - θ \\

\cot\left(\dfrac{13\pi}{20}\right)

This is especially helpful when writing trigonometric ratios in terms of reference angles, as we usually need to determine which quadrant the angle lies in.

Let's express the following trigonometric ratio in terms of a reference angle:

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)
$$

You might find it tricky to visualize this angle straight off the bat. So, let's start by converting the angle measure into degrees.

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by

$$
\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}
$$

This gives

$$
\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac {180^\circ} {\pi}\right) = 120^\circ
$$

Therefore

$$
\dfrac{2\pi}{3}
$$

is equivalent to $120^\circ$, which lies in the $2$nd quadrant.

![](images/34/342602449228f93042121b22f39d6cc203a6d945934a9ddb726e862838832815.png)

Now, to express

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)
$$

in terms of $\sin\theta_R$, we follow three steps:

1. Find its reference angle $\theta_R$.
2. Calculate the value of the function for $\theta_R$.
3. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

**Step 1**: Since

$$
\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}
$$

is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle $\theta_R$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
θ_{R} &= π - θ \\
&= π - \frac{2π}{3} \\
&= \frac{3π}{3} - \frac{2π}{3} \\
&= \frac{π}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)
$$

, and therefore we're interested in

$$
\sin\theta_R = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)
$$

**Step 3:** The ratio

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)
$$

must be *positive* because the sine ratio is *always* positive in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)
$$

And we're done!

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-x-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-x-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy-1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](images/c3/c3ec90119193ca9c0cb886bc7b7c698eb155e6a801fd267c0a17a0d329eff84d.png)

Starting with ![](images/ef/eff9e5b8ab46002bd82fa42d59f60b1bb78ca04228d7c73b52d131d222ccb894.png) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2xy-1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}y-x-2 \\ x{y}^{2}-y+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(1)(2)-1 & (1)^{2} \\ (2)^{2} & 2(1)(2)-1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{2}(2)-1-2 \\ 1(2)^{2}-2+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 3-4\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 13\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{11}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.2 \\ -0.6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050483} {:db/id 17592186204498 :question/id #uuid "83394f73-0e0c-509d-afc6-c9fbe175f1ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-256200"} {:db/id 17592186204509 :question/id #uuid "5800980a-2f76-57ac-b91f-63be30605046" :question/math-academy-id "q-256559" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204082 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e0dc557b-f9f5-5dfc-a860-a47b76b4fc42" :knowledge-point/title "Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "d5af280c-c756-592a-9a39-676c0b8ff81b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203013} {:answer-field/id #uuid "4f26550d-f8be-5b43-b6c1-b97ec83cf43b" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203014}] :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x, y)$ in the region $[1, 2] \cdot [1, 2]⊆R^{2}$, where

\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](images/95/95e234c5c9b32e1ea965f1cd184563699fbd2793d51a9d1e4ec96ffb4e42dc50.png)

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+y-4 \\ x+{y}^{2}-3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(3) & 1 \\ 1 & 2(-1)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{2}+(-1)-4 \\ 3+(-1)^{2}-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{30}{13} \\ -\frac{11}{13}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}2.308 \\ -0.846\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186204499 :question/id #uuid "e2d3b902-846f-5938-a220-235340dd6162" :question/math-academy-id "q-256226" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204083 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bad338b3-41cf-5193-aef7-d73c8f859c69" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "87e64f3c-51b1-5434-ba7f-f814d56f0237" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186202982}] :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x, y)$ in the region $[1, 2] \cdot [1, 2]⊆R^{2}$, where

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](images/13/13f9eb9850462317be5a5c7da22fe53ee89b24d9ce1a9226c2d0ee1e6355ba19.png)

$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](images/d5/d5eb5a91fdd96bf6ca50539d2119a97ce9e5600b3114f708cda4d95a047e8b81.png) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.25 \\ -0.25\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.25 \\ -0.25\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.75 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting  at the point $[1,\,1]^{T},$ and compute the components of the first iteration, rounding your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).

| $[$ | {{field-1}} | $2$ | $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ | {{field-2}} | $]$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| {{field-3}} | $3$ | $-1$ |  |  |  |

| ${x}_{1}≈[$ | $0.833$ | $]$ |

| {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4x & 2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2 \\ {x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1) & 2(1) \\ 3(1)^{2} & 3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}2(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}-2 \\ (1)^{3}+(1)^{3}-1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-0.166\,66… \\ -0.166\,66…\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.833 \\ 0.833\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186204502 :question/id #uuid "d65c1411-1261-569b-b79c-90235ce25c18" :question/math-academy-id "q-256287"} {:db/id 17592186292573 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205019 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205143 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how Newton’s method works for functions of a single variable. Given a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the method generates a sequence of approximations using the rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

This formula uses the derivative $f'(x_n)$ to construct a local linear approximation of $f$ near $x_n$, which we then use to refine our guess.

In this lesson, we turn to the multivariable case, where we want to solve systems of nonlinear equations. Specifically, we are interested in finding a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ that solves

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},
$$

for a vector-valued function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$.

The multivariable version of Newton’s method updates our guess using the formula

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $\boldsymbol{f}$, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n$.

This is a natural extension of the single-variable rule, replacing the derivative with the Jacobian and the scalar update with a vector.

To see how this method works in practice, let’s walk through a concrete example.

 The formula for Newton's method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function [math]\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n[/math] is

\[
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
\]

in the region $[-2, 2] \times [-2, 2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$.

We will perform one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method, starting from the initial guess

$$

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(1)^{3} & -2(1) \\ 2(1) & -3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{4}-(1)^{2}+5 \\ (1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{4\cdot (-3)-(-2)\cdot 2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}-13 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.625 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

is not always the most practical way for us to compute the next step. In higher dimensions, it’s often more useful to avoid calculating the inverse of a large matrix by rewriting the update as a linear system instead.

Let’s go through how we can do that step by step.

We start with the standard Newton update

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

Next, we subtract $\mathbf{x}_n$ from both sides

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n = - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

Then, we multiply both sides by $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)$

$$
J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This gives us the *linear system form* of Newton’s method. This equivalent form allows us to solve directly for the update direction $\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n$ without ever computing the inverse of the Jacobian.

To better understand how the method works in practice, let’s walk through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad00df1c-99b0-5fa7-96ee-f43a94557f73" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10905 :tutorial/title "Alternative to Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions Using Linear Systems"} :step/id #uuid "16956ca3-9f37-53de-bdb3-838d68b2c7f4" :step/math-academy-id 460088 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205024}} {:db/id 17592186205024 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205202 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are looking for a zero of the function

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

in the region $[-2, 2] \times [-2, 3] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$.

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Starting with $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1)^{3} & -2(1) \\ 2(1) & -3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{4}-(1)^{2}+5 \\ (1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let’s solve this system using Gaussian elimination. We first set $\begin{bmatrix}{d}_{1} \\ {d}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$, so the system becomes

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

We write the augmented matrix as

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -5 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate the entry below the leading $4$, we perform the row operation $R_2 := R_2 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & -2 & 1.5\end{aligned}
$$

From the second row, we get

$$
-2d_2 = 1.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad d_2 = -0.75.
$$

We then substitute this into the first row, which gives

$$
4d_1 - 2(-0.75) = -5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 4d_1 = -6.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad d_1 = -1.625.
$$

So, the update vector is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix}
$$

Hence, our updated approximation of the root is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.625 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a7de67ce-53d0-56ee-aa95-84dde9560679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13126 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "aac6d91b-f746-5467-8c5a-9b33cfe7ff06" :step/math-academy-id 460089 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205025}} {:db/id 17592186205025 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204084 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203827 :question/id #uuid "5da362d4-cb58-5b51-acc0-582e3a0d42e4" :question/math-academy-id "e-16571"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f12c74b6-ac99-514f-96c4-a26e8fef6028" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049422}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204494} {:db/id 17592186204502} {:db/id 17592186292573} {:db/id 17592186292574} {:db/id 17592186292579} {:db/id 17592186365460} {:db/id 17592186365467} {:db/id 17592186365474}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method Using Linear Systems"} :step/id #uuid "1cc729fd-23d2-528a-b73a-daf856e2f710" :step/math-academy-id 460090 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205026}} {:db/id 17592186205026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205205 :tutorial/content "Just like in the single-variable case, the idea is to simplify the problem by replacing a nonlinear function with its linear approximation near our current guess.

Suppose we want to solve a system of nonlinear equations

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},
$$

where $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector-valued function.

Near a point $\mathbf{x}_0$, we approximate $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ using its first-order Taylor expansion:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0),
$$

where $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $\boldsymbol{f}$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0$.

Since this linear approximation is valid near $\mathbf{x}_0$, we solve the simpler system

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}
$$

instead of the full nonlinear system.

To find the next guess $\mathbf{x}_1$, we solve this linear system for $\mathbf{x}$. We isolate the term $\mathbf{x}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}({x}_{0})(x-{x}_{0}) & =-f({x}_{0}) \\ x-{x}_{0} & =-[{J}_{f}({x}_{0})]^{-1}f({x}_{0}) \\ x & ={x}_{0}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{0})]^{-1}f({x}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

This new value becomes our next guess, which we call $\mathbf{x}_1$. So, we write

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This is the multivariable version of the Newton–Raphson update rule." :tutorial/id #uuid "729dee84-09dc-5611-8787-27a3cc455d8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13227 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "b5c82352-d99e-5c17-9e33-330fd65ee50e" :step/math-academy-id 460093}] :activity/title "Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204161} {:db/id 17592186205019 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205143 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how Newton’s method works for functions of a single variable. $$

$$

This formula uses the derivative $f'(x_n)$ to construct a local linear approximation of $f$ near $x_n$, which we then use to refine our guess.

In this lesson, we turn to the multivariable case, where we want to solve systems of nonlinear equations. Specifically, we are interested in finding a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ that solves

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},
$$

for a vector-valued function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$.

$$

$$

where $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $\boldsymbol{f}$, evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n$.

This is a natural extension of the single-variable rule, replacing the derivative with the Jacobian and the scalar update with a vector.

\]

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e9a1704a-b2f2-58ca-8eb8-cfe28a10b296" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13125 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186205021 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204082 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203825 :question/id #uuid "37f0d2c0-c174-5478-a007-5fb3d32bafe2" :question/math-academy-id "e-16569"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e0dc557b-f9f5-5dfc-a860-a47b76b4fc42" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050483}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204498} {:db/id 17592186204509} {:db/id 17592186292571} {:db/id 17592186292576} {:db/id 17592186292577} {:db/id 17592186292589}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method"} :step/id #uuid "e285dc9f-9805-5b95-bd83-c6f8da901a74" :step/math-academy-id 460082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205022}} {:db/id 17592186205022 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204083 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203826 :question/id #uuid "1fa3ed18-5fb9-53b2-a067-5db623a289d3" :question/math-academy-id "e-16570"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bad338b3-41cf-5193-aef7-d73c8f859c69" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204499} {:db/id 17592186204500} {:db/id 17592186292581} {:db/id 17592186292583} {:db/id 17592186292585} {:db/id 17592186292588} {:db/id 17592186365483} {:db/id 17592186365486}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method"} :step/id #uuid "9429df1a-24e6-5bf3-ba31-93d9bf4d2b34" :step/math-academy-id 460085 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205023}} {:db/id 17592186205023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205157 :tutorial/content "Now that we’ve seen how to apply Newton’s method in the multivariable case, it’s worth noting that the standard update formula

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)
$$

is not always the most practical way for us to compute the next step. In higher dimensions, it’s often more useful to avoid calculating the inverse of a large matrix by rewriting the update as a linear system instead.

Let’s go through how we can do that step by step.

We start with the standard Newton update

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

Next, we subtract $\mathbf{x}_n$ from both sides

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n = - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

Then, we multiply both sides by $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)$

$$
J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This gives us the *linear system form* of Newton’s method. This equivalent form allows us to solve directly for the update direction $\mathbf{x}_{n+1} - \mathbf{x}_n$ without ever computing the inverse of the Jacobian.

To better understand how the method works in practice, let’s walk through a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad00df1c-99b0-5fa7-96ee-f43a94557f73" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10905 :tutorial/title "Alternative to Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions Using Linear Systems"} {:db/id 17592186205024 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205202 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are looking for a zero of the function

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

in the region $[-2, 2] \times [-2, 3] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$.

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Starting with $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4(1)^{3} & -2(1) \\ 2(1) & -3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{4}-(1)^{2}+5 \\ (1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let’s solve this system using Gaussian elimination. We first set $\begin{bmatrix}{d}_{1} \\ {d}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$, so the system becomes

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

We write the augmented matrix as

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -5 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate the entry below the leading $4$, we perform the row operation $R_2 := R_2 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & -2 & 1.5\end{aligned}
$$

From the second row, we get

$$
-2d_2 = 1.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad d_2 = -0.75.
$$

We then substitute this into the first row, which gives

$$
4d_1 - 2(-0.75) = -5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 4d_1 = -6.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad d_1 = -1.625.
$$

So, the update vector is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix}
$$

Hence, our updated approximation of the root is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1.625 \\ -0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.625 \\ 0.25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a7de67ce-53d0-56ee-aa95-84dde9560679" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13126 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "aac6d91b-f746-5467-8c5a-9b33cfe7ff06" :step/math-academy-id 460089 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205025}} {:db/id 17592186205202 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are looking for a zero of the function

Suppose we want to solve a system of nonlinear equations

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},
$$

where $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector-valued function.

Near a point $\mathbf{x}_0$, we approximate $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})$ using its first-order Taylor expansion:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0),
$$

where $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $\boldsymbol{f}$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0$.

Since this linear approximation is valid near $\mathbf{x}_0$, we solve the simpler system

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}
$$

instead of the full nonlinear system.

To find the next guess $\mathbf{x}_1$, we solve this linear system for $\mathbf{x}$. We isolate the term $\mathbf{x}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}({x}_{0})(x-{x}_{0}) & =-f({x}_{0}) \\ x-{x}_{0} & =-[{J}_{f}({x}_{0})]^{-1}f({x}_{0}) \\ x & ={x}_{0}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{0})]^{-1}f({x}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

This new value becomes our next guess, which we call $\mathbf{x}_1$. So, we write

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

This is the multivariable version of the Newton–Raphson update rule." :tutorial/id #uuid "729dee84-09dc-5611-8787-27a3cc455d8e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13227 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "b5c82352-d99e-5c17-9e33-330fd65ee50e" :step/math-academy-id 460093} {:db/id 17592186205205 :tutorial/content "Just like in the single-variable case, the idea is to simplify the problem by replacing a nonlinear function with its linear approximation near our current guess.

:topic/math-academy-id 1001} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186093085 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093360 :tutorial/content "Consider the polar curves $r=2(1+\cos\theta)$ and $r=2.$ What is the area of the shaded region shown below?

![](images/c0/c011bf3b40639e10ec151541d0892d5095b2d983b6ed03247824f06f225c10d9.png)

First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],$ namely

$$
\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer curve}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner curve}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta,
$$

In our case, we have

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ 

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/7b/7b77af383d0d05d00c91db364e17675dfd45445eb5ac8e2926f8bb90220bc0fe.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2(1+\cos\theta).$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}({(2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ))}^{2}-{2}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(4(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )-4)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "87bcd4b8-6965-56b9-8f60-65d778fe217c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1138 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "644bccac-3cde-5911-bd4c-a81e0ad52e7f" :step/math-academy-id 17592186093360 :tutorial/content "Consider the polar curves $r=2(1+\cos\theta)$ and $r=2.$ What is the area of the shaded region shown below?

![](images/c0/c011bf3b40639e10ec151541d0892d5095b2d983b6ed03247824f06f225c10d9.png)

First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],$ namely

$$
\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer curve}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner curve}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta,
$$

In our case, we have

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ 

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/7b/7b77af383d0d05d00c91db364e17675dfd45445eb5ac8e2926f8bb90220bc0fe.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=2(1+\cos\theta).$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}({(2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ))}^{2}-{2}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(4(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )-4)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "87bcd4b8-6965-56b9-8f60-65d778fe217c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1138 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "644bccac-3cde-5911-bd4c-a81e0ad52e7f" :step/math-academy-id 645939 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093139}} {:db/id 17592186093360 :tutorial/content "Consider the polar curves $r=2(1+\cos\theta)$ and $r=2.$ What is the area of the shaded region shown below?

:knowledge-point/title "Computing an Integral Using the Sum Rule"}] :question/problem "Find the integral of $x^2 + 1$." :question/worked-solution "Applying the sum rule, we compute the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\intx^{2} + 1dx &= \intx^{2}dx + \int1dx \\
&= \intx^{2}dx + \intx^{0}dx \\
&= (\frac{x^{2 + 1}}{2 + 1}) + x + C \\
&= \frac{1}{3}x^{3} + x + C
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049481} {:db/id 17592186184549 :question/id #uuid "ebf755a0-1ba0-54d7-8cfa-097d44473af4" :question/math-academy-id "q-2159"} {:db/id 17592186184738 :question/id #uuid "bd6f191d-dd25-52a7-91ee-5275c10c8293" :question/math-academy-id "q-29828"} {:db/id 17592186233186 :question/id #uuid "8d0c3f56-ed74-5e4d-bb18-eac56541b5e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-113781"} {:db/id 17592186234302 :question/id #uuid "79aa6724-ce36-5977-907b-506fab54c4d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71169" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186184153 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0db9b1c3-1e31-53f6-9fc2-1c611e2f9398" :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Integral Using the Sum Rule"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the integral of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}+4.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the sum rule, we compute the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}+4\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}x+4\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\text{d}x+4\int {x}^{0}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+4(\frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1})+C \\  & =-2\cdot {x}^{-1/2}+4x+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}+4x+C\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186234303 :question/id #uuid "09d58888-0116-53f3-b47a-9d0d7153229f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71173"} {:db/id 17592186541108 :question/id #uuid "836e24be-b58e-500b-bb05-e9b2030ce5e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-133291"} {:db/id 17592186184154 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184058 :question/id #uuid "ea7dadee-2b44-5e62-bef4-26fb0cb185ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-372"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a58c0a18-4221-50f1-b31c-ae58d099d79d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048442}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184548 :question/id #uuid "a6758c57-4a70-5cd7-8c06-6fcee40efe7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-211"} {:db/id 17592186184550 :question/id #uuid "74b8affd-5a59-5349-9045-109c73cdc246" :question/math-academy-id "q-2166"} {:db/id 17592186233643 :question/id #uuid "6b6e2582-e861-5aac-850f-2f62d29905a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-2251"} {:db/id 17592186233755 :question/id #uuid "0bf78498-fa41-5c5b-8e73-bc357aed8c2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-29825"} {:db/id 17592186235391 :question/id #uuid "3c85a07f-1862-53e2-9986-87c4ee966897" :question/math-academy-id "q-132983"} {:db/id 17592186235456 :question/id #uuid "221f7f46-e501-5c4b-9474-541896c7450d" :question/math-academy-id "q-167635"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Integral Using the Sum and Constant Factor Rules"} {:db/id 17592186184058 :question/id #uuid "ea7dadee-2b44-5e62-bef4-26fb0cb185ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-372" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186184154 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a58c0a18-4221-50f1-b31c-ae58d099d79d" :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Integral Using the Sum and Constant Factor Rules"}] :question/problem "Calculate $\displaystyle \int 2 x^3 - x \,\textrm d x$." :question/worked-solution "Using the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int(5(\sqrt{x})^{3} - 4x^{2} + 5)dx &= \int(5x^{3/2} - 4x^{2} + 5)dx \\
&= 5\intx^{3/2}dx - 4\intx^{2}dx + 5\int1dx \\
&= 5(\frac{x^{5/2}}{\frac{5}{2}}) - 4(\frac{x^{3}}{3}) + 5(x) + C \\
&= 5 \cdot \frac{2}{5}x^{5/2} - \frac{4}{3}x^{3} + 5x + C \\
&= 2\sqrt{x^{5}} - \frac{4}{3}x^{3} + 5x + C
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186184563 :question/id #uuid "564c4689-85ae-5d46-8778-645d30c6800f" :question/math-academy-id "q-2250"} {:db/id 17592186184739 :question/id #uuid 17592186184906 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185366 :tutorial/content "How can we calculate the integral of a sum of functions, like $\displaystyle \int (x+x^3)\,\textrm d x$?

According to the **sum rule**, the integral of the sum of functions is equal to the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\int (f(x) \pm g(x))\,\textrm d x = \int f(x) \,\textrm d x \pm \int g(x) \,\textrm d x
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int(x + x^{3})dx &= \intxdx + \intx^{3}dx \\
&= (\frac{x^{2}}{2} + c_{1}) + (\frac{x^{4}}{4} + c_{2}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + \frac{1}{4}x^{4} + (c_{1} + c_{2}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + \frac{1}{4}x^{4} + C
\end{aligned}
$$

where we renamed

$$
c_1+c_2=C
$$

(The sum of two arbitrary constants is itself an arbitrary constant.)" :tutorial/id #uuid "207bbd12-158a-58be-b000-82cace6dcdde" :tutorial/math-academy-id 701 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "61a29b78-51b2-509a-bb12-5c2009c1ee92" :step/math-academy-id 1351 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184907}} {:db/id 17592186184907 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184153 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184057 :question/id #uuid "e4a94ca8-82ee-5776-a46d-b735d4ab60fb" :question/math-academy-id "e-371"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0db9b1c3-1e31-53f6-9fc2-1c611e2f9398" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049481}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184549} {:db/id 17592186184738} {:db/id 17592186233186} {:db/id 17592186234302} {:db/id 17592186234303} {:db/id 17592186541108}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Integral Using the Sum Rule"} :step/id #uuid "319d1f65-0963-5490-81bd-5f970237cb5a" :step/math-academy-id 1352 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184908}} {:db/id 17592186184908 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185367 :tutorial/content "For more complicated functions consisting of the sum of functions multiplied by constants, we can combine the constant factor and sum rules as follows:

of $x$ that satisfy $2<2x+4\le 6$ and $4x>12.$" :question/worked-solution "To solve compound "and" inequalities, we solve each inequality separately and then find their intersection.

- First, we solve $2<2x+4\le 6\,:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & <2x+4\le 6 \\ 2-4 & <2x+4-4\le 6-4 \\ -2 & <2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-2}{2} & <\frac{2x}{2}\le \frac{2}{2} \\ -1 & <x\le 1\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/48/485e77fe84f5745120d5f450c3e1043ee61463a83f7c12bfc6d1ae0e4124a38b.png)

   

- Then, we solve  $4x>12\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & >12 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & >\frac{12}{4} \\ x & >3\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/65/654f97a64ec1a13b4a94860dfa07d05f7c119a5fe2084ba23aa994a97f0bea70.png)

To find the values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](images/d2/d2d0f41792356b6c250612b033413f66bfd7a35440e1b84da660fccd5c1285b0.png)

$$

$$

It turns out that the solutions do not overlap at all. Therefore, there are no values of $x$ that satisfy both inequalities simultaneously. $$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=0 \\ y+2z &=0 \\ z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form.

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186416435 :question/id #uuid "2ad315bd-aaaa-532d-a173-690fb5924119" :question/math-academy-id "q-131586"} {:db/id 17592186096675 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$

$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-5z &=1 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z &=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2y-3z-2 \\ y &=y \\ z &=z,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+2y-4z &=4 \\ -x+y-2z &=2 \\ x-y+2z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system." :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -4 & 4 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -4 & 4 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=y-2z-2 \\ y &=y \\ z &=z,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y-2z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1049} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097522 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097843 :tutorial/content "Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/7c/7c2283c7de572acfc58b443499598554ecf3d26b1a13c48c80b8d6aadf7b576a.svg)

The matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form, but we can transform it even further into the **reduced row echelon form** (RREF) using the standard **Gauss-Jordan** method. 

The algorithm is similar to the algorithm of converting a matrix to row echelon form, except that we need to make *all* the pivot entries equal to $1$ and *all* the entries below *and above* a pivot (in a pivot column) equal to $0.$

In our case, we convert $M$ to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final matrix is in reduced row echelon form:

- all the pivot entries are equal to $1$ (here we have $\color{red}1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- all the entries below and above a pivot are equal to ${\color{blue}0}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ce056e74-9707-52d3-b172-483ca14e1f8f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3160 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "78885948-fa6f-5f46-8f96-e5da861960dd" :step/math-academy-id 17209 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097523}} {:db/id 17592186097523 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097844 :tutorial/content "For a $3\times 3$ system with $3$ pivots, the Gauss-Jordan method can be described as follows:

- First, reduce the matrix to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination method (also making all pivot entries equal to $1$). 
![](images/5c/5c0f5ac3d95843b142c90e8ce83378ea2b2ad693baba6670e0cde46a449f5225.svg)

- We use the third row and necessary row operations to make the entries above $a_{33}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{23} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{23})R_3$, and

- if $a_{13} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1 + (-a_{13})R_3$.

- We use the second row and necessary row operations to make the entries above $a_{22}$ equal to $0$. Namely, 

- if $a_{12} \neq 0$, then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1 + (-a_{12})R_2$.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to reduced row echelon form.

![](images/9c/9c817628a3c646a928f12548a109b8136bb0a5977fab6e4d18e972690d81159b.svg)

**Note:** Unlike the row echelon form, the *reduced* row echelon form of a matrix is unique." :tutorial/id #uuid "f74e6075-9c2a-5495-ab21-470711559f2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3161 :tutorial/title
