"df6c8a6d-153a-5484-848d-1043ee95c582" :question/math-academy-id "q-74621" :question/problem "Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x-11y+5z &=-1 \\ x-3y+2z &=1 \\ -3x+9y-6z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form." :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -11 & 5 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & -11 & 5 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & -11 & 5 & -1 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ -3 & 9 & -6 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the row echelon form above, we have only two pivots (in the $1$st and $2$nd columns). To transform the matrix to reduced row echelon form, we need to create zeros above the pivots only. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -7 & -14 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "06ed1b32-abf8-5d02-b409-e83aa1a9bf69" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422482}} {:db/id 17592186422481 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097174 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f53140c-1654-5c33-b318-d2cc5cdbf3e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186416405} {:answer/id #uuid "3b8ed053-8c5f-5809-b29d-46bc30062dd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,-2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186416409} {:answer/id #uuid "52ed3b97-c09d-5bac-bedf-d8cb30fd9295" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,-3,1⟩" :db/id 17592186416411} {:answer/id #uuid "ad204329-d0a2-52cb-bab5-d155cba3473f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-3,-2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186416423} {:answer/id #uuid "fa5e31d8-6742-527d-a027-3e41d829bbd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-3,-2,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186416428}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186416409} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d9c6d72-c8a0-5fe2-aea3-51adff0f94d5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186416431}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb5d2e37-01c6-52dc-86a3-0e3d22b79684" :question/math-academy-id "q-20267" :question/problem "Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=2 \\ x+2y+z &=0 \\ x+y+2z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system." :question/worked-solution "The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3 \\ y &=-2 \\ z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we have the solution $x=3$, $y=-2$, and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨3,-2,1⟩.$"} :step/id #uuid "1f437206-fa08-5382-b319-4b882827b9a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422483}} {:db/id 17592186422482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186266102 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "083caf03-1501-5cba-8190-446a66b010a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,3,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186263075} {:answer/id #uuid "9af8bfe2-063c-5dba-b504-5816b98f9766" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,-3,0⟩" :db/id 17592186264325} {:answer/id #uuid "b8b913e9-5eb2-5d55-9bc3-2f3b88be543b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,-3,1⟩" :db/id 17592186264598} {:answer/id #uuid "da1a8356-2e88-513c-b7fa-151c2d4478c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,-2,0⟩" :db/id 17592186264902} {:answer/id #uuid "f5e3c0bf-feab-56d8-8788-d7833ba1031b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,3,0⟩" :db/id 17592186265152}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264325} :answer-field/id #uuid "71bd9945-c16d-52b1-9144-9035edc43bba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265440}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8ff5175c-29cf-5e1c-8b8a-50a809738a87" :question/math-academy-id "q-131618" :question/problem "Consider the following system of linear equations:

Using a Difference of Squares"}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- $P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[4, 6]$

- $P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2, 6]$

Calculate  $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j,$ where $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ and $\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j.
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ is just the length of the interval $[2, 6].$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=6-2=4.\end{aligned}
$$

For the sum over $i,$ we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i} & =({x}_{1}+{x}_{0})Δ{x}_{1}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{1})Δ{x}_{2}+⋯+({x}_{m}+{x}_{m-1})Δ{x}_{m} \\  & =({x}_{1}\,+\,{x}_{0})({x}_{1}\,-\,{x}_{0})+({x}_{2}\,+\,{x}_{1})({x}_{2}\,-\,{x}_{1})+({x}_{m}\,+\,{x}_{m-1})({x}_{m}\,-\,{x}_{m-1}) \\  & =({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})+({x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{m-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}}-{x}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{x}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-\cancel{{x}_{m-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{x}_{0}^{2}+{x}_{m}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={6}^{2}-{4}^{2} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we finally arrive at 

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j = 20\cdot 4 = 80.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049943} {:db/id 17592186180268 :question/id #uuid "a88af1ba-c0a1-5207-b3ae-5df258155f41" :question/math-academy-id "q-72129"} {:db/id 17592186180269 :question/id #uuid "9ed12378-3e1d-529d-b73a-027163d47330" :question/math-academy-id "q-72481" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179666 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5ee41f2-7116-52f4-b1f7-923997d994ab" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "84152621-f04a-5e4b-a8a7-665644579b58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186179159} {:answer/id #uuid "ac8792b9-e35e-5c3a-8c30-520e6d3e6702" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186179160} {:answer/id #uuid "fd77f5cb-dbff-5066-a8f2-ae463d81e8c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186179161} {:answer/id #uuid "28d5ae24-8e40-55a7-8e5d-46ec21f816ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186179162} {:answer/id #uuid "3598869e-7494-5767-9dba-d392f97d24a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186179163}] :answer-field/id #uuid "68242cd7-719b-5707-a713-aa2924f886ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186179158}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}-2({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
-2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ is just the length of the interval $[-2,1].$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=1-(-2) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

For the sum over $i,$ we evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i} & =({x}_{1}+{x}_{0})Δ{x}_{1}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{1})Δ{x}_{2}+⋯+({x}_{m}+{x}_{m-1})Δ{x}_{n} \\  & =({x}_{1}\,+\,{x}_{0})({x}_{1}\,-\,{x}_{0})\,+\,({x}_{2}\,+\,{x}_{1})({x}_{2}\,-\,{x}_{1})\,+\,⋯\,+\,({x}_{m}\,+\,{x}_{m-1})({x}_{m}\,-\,{x}_{m-1}) \\  & =({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})+({x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{m-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}}-{x}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{x}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{x}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({x}_{m}^{2}-\cancel{{x}_{m-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{x}_{0}^{2}+{x}_{m}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(-1)^{2}-(-3)^{2} \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

$$
-2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}({x}_{i}+{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=(-2)\cdot (-8)\cdot 3=48.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186526049 :question/id #uuid "8659922e-fb1c-5be1-95b0-fc0ad4f5b044" :question/math-academy-id "q-149632"} {:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179584 :question/id #uuid "e2f01953-2fb1-5ddb-83ae-5d8a73e7f7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-9482"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048800} {:db/id 17592186049629}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179979 :question/id #uuid "7cb18f0a-5793-5799-850f-ef66cbf9de18" :question/math-academy-id "q-122867"} {:db/id 17592186180267 :question/id #uuid "b8ba4a0f-f607-55a9-9beb-85f51bad2770" :question/math-academy-id "q-72128"} {:db/id 17592186256777 :question/id #uuid "ecb6ed16-6d45-5080-8683-a8fbdb3fa178" :question/math-academy-id "q-123069"} {:db/id 17592186275216 :question/id #uuid "ba5f3cf2-5db7-5ec1-b7c9-a70950beee5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-149628"} {:db/id 17592186339124 :question/id #uuid "9f73aa4c-df24-5091-bd74-35aefea94a85" :question/math-academy-id "q-72476"} {:db/id 17592186339125 :question/id #uuid "d6d7f627-89ab-505d-97fc-50a07131d61d" :question/math-academy-id "q-72479"} {:db/id 17592186525988 :question/id #uuid "18882139-e768-512f-b798-8450fe515622" :question/math-academy-id "q-123070"} {:db/id 17592186526042 :question/id #uuid "77ce5f28-3326-5c6e-a417-40662b67aeff" :question/math-academy-id "q-123067"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"} {:db/id 17592186179584 :question/id #uuid "e2f01953-2fb1-5ddb-83ae-5d8a73e7f7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-9482" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"}] :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

- $P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[-1, 2]$

- $P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2, 3]$

Calculate $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,$ where $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ and $\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[-1, 2]$ and $[2,3]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-(-1)=3, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,5]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[1,5]$ and $[5,7]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =5-1=4, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =7-5=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=4\cdot 2=8.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186526042 :question/id #uuid "77ce5f28-3326-5c6e-a417-40662b67aeff" :question/math-academy-id "q-123067" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179722 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f913fab-d0b5-5e9e-b292-039afe4a148c" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "294c3cc6-d662-53c9-b36e-6a5692b9f4aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186525306} {:answer/id #uuid "2fb1fc71-c6c9-501e-95e7-d1d36b4e13d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186525319} {:answer/id #uuid "9bb97fb7-9081-5e35-a39a-0d9ff39f247c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186525602} {:answer/id #uuid "afe570cc-99d0-5bbc-a39e-c80b3ab0abf6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186525650} {:answer/id #uuid "b26a0da6-fba9-5626-a287-a7c4aa41e02a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186525662}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "294c3cc6-d662-53c9-b36e-6a5692b9f4aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186525306} :answer-field/id #uuid "eb3c82ed-1671-54bd-8e2d-7967feacedd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186525966}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following partitions:

![](images/b2/b2b9753f603902f8fc3b86c7bc58c927fca6e25c26b018ce85e665b47d75b77b.png)

We can describe the entire rectangle as ![](images/d6/d6e3d65ec5ef708e7d2f8368b43f0b05b2f0488b533a3ff6b46fd8297505894e.svg) where ![](images/66/66d58377d47e96b8baecdfbc2c2365f86825f2e43e17dfaac2225d1de20191c1.svg) denotes the Cartesian product.

Now, let's partition ![](images/08/085f4d77675f3cb7323d94feaa9eaa38f2fecb26c0f8483895f9ddf36b8d319d.svg) into ![](images/37/37e17c4a2302e6352fb7186621c9c43bb5e99d43a8a0bc700c0181d36c6cc915.svg) rectangles of equal area, as shown below.

![](images/10/10c85c7b9034a7cd342c5360a13eca471b103e769415a3459e7841c3d948ee7d.png)

Note that we can describe our partition without a diagram as follows:

- The partition of the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-interval ![](images/10/10afad0ff28bd2c5b5f3450dd6a83c4c6263cf628e8f405c7ff0d06ed7249072.svg) can be expressed as ![](images/bf/bf81cbc93793a83bbd68b3de440efd7329b8979e6ad9ca76a755938ba1079955.svg) where ![](images/67/674ac6553524f5663674850d81bea00ec8c59ee651fd2f4c942e0ab0a8a5d790.svg) ![](images/44/44fabdac948e1c3466dde55f202f25d1c267c85e22f0d38d8a1deed12ce2a929.svg) ![](images/5a/5ad873e1f6b4b1ba4a7810e18f8ab571d5bd3f8aaa4d72401c7bd19721a389e3.svg) and ![](images/f0/f0b8129f0d98db64a6be3240f33cf4b91e651fa2f2329d0258beba183624a977.svg)

- The partition of the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-interval ![](images/2e/2e43b93bdeca20a22541e4b289efb7e37f3b6a391bfed32323c4e3a3c7cda162.svg) can be expressed as ![](images/c3/c38a1873b3c68a6d204981670a7360f59512b1b42ce835b795b6be24619a2a6a.svg) where ![](images/a9/a92c357a02416f0914aa679bd177f1d72f7b52e2f063371fe36d8db0b2a0ead6.svg) ![](images/7a/7afd61dbfbaad2470afc104718dd99118e9f4cbfa82a63b4d0abb0b2563179c7.svg) and ![](images/4a/4a6fda6532f4b6963586cfbcb6c3d2174940834d2ed22645497d48f0788ba384.svg)

- The partition of the entire rectangle can be described as ![](images/17/174f77031e6ccf34569f7b02648f9199b402a08898161efc74bff691c34faf5b.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "e8975bb9-0b71-53a4-98ad-d358801bde48" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5780 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b0d06c7f-0e78-510d-8852-82dea5166908" :step/math-academy-id 35499 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180472}} {:db/id 17592186180472 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180710 :tutorial/content "We have our partition $P = P_1\times P_2,$ shown below.

![](images/0e/0e497b6d43e4d46d4fad71bc2b81810c972b0e306817d161ad3a2e285e6b9d6e.png)

Let $\Delta x_i$ be the difference in the $x$-values of any two successive points in $P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
$$

Similarly, let $\Delta y_j$ be the difference in the $y$-values of any two successive points in $P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}
$$

It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j
$$

Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

- Here, the $x_i$'s partition the interval $[1,4]$ which has length $4 - 1 = 3.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.$

- Similarly, the $y_j$'s partition the interval $[2,4]$ which has length $4 - 2 = 2.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3$ represents the width of the rectangle, while $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2$ represents the height.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j$ represents the area of the rectangle." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e13206a-d7f4-54d7-aa8c-37e9c0e3d26c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5798 :tutorial/title "Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition"} :step/id #uuid "b2095dad-9a02-54e5-a167-0babe1804a2a" :step/math-academy-id 35548 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180463}}] :activity/title "Calculating Double Summations Over Partitions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179852} {:db/id 17592186180466 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180707 :tutorial/content "Just as we can form partitions of closed intervals of the real line, we can also partition rectangular regions in the Cartesian plane.

By assuming that all of the side faces have the same height $(8\,\text{in})$, find the total surface area of the square pyramid above by considering its net." :question/worked-solution "The net of our pyramid is as follows:

![](images/c4/c4a5fe995aaaf47b7ab2b90492059d739fc2352955dc1e12a71852fc13046a33.png)

First, notice that the base of the pyramid is a square with sides equal to $5 \, \text{in}$. Therefore, we have

$$
\text{Area of square} = 5 \times 5 = 25 \, \text{in}^2
$$

Each side face of our solid is triangle, where the base is $5\,\text{in}$ and the height is $8\,\text{in}$. Therefore, we have

$$
\text{Area of triangle} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 8 = 20 \, \text{in}^2
$$

Finally, the surface area of the pyramid consists of $1$ square (the base) and $4$ triangles (the side faces).

Adding the areas, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
Surface area &= 1 \cdot (Area of the square) + 4 \cdot (Area of the triangle) \\
&= 1 \cdot 25 + 4 \cdot 20 \\
&= 25 + 80 \\
&= 105in^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186147974 :question/id #uuid "8ce742b5-57f4-53b1-882f-51d5011e4a65" :question/math-academy-id "q-62256"} {:db/id 17592186148152 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+1} & ={2}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\ln \left( e^a \right) = a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 =\ln \left(2^{x}\cdot 5\right)
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180141 :question/id #uuid "3a4d2c64-ecf2-540e-86cd-1d47fbb20b4c" :question/math-academy-id "q-233243"} {:db/id 17592186180154 :question/id #uuid "06c172b1-e1bb-5a05-93ab-4ac5b7da1eda" :question/math-academy-id "q-26390"} {:db/id 17592186247138 :question/id #uuid "27f7c13c-66f0-53e5-b54c-76ef4dcb10ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-110545"} {:db/id 17592186290534 :question/id #uuid "f1f31343-a477-520d-bcc1-1e38225689fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-242902" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179788 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5eb24b54-bdb8-5269-bd38-d346a52bbc6e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c5012993-bc88-5829-a54b-d1ece2e35800" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\operatorname{ln}(2)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}(2)}" :db/id 17592186289335}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c5012993-bc88-5829-a54b-d1ece2e35800" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\operatorname{ln}(2)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}(2)}" :db/id 17592186289335} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f169737-4695-5e9f-9c2c-725e6eebea72" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186290082}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, determine the value of $x$ that satisfies the equation ${e}^{x+2}={2}^{x+3}.$

:question/worked-solution "First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+2} & ={9}^{x-2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x-2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(x+2)\ln(5) = (x-2)\ln(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\ x & =\frac{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9))}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180144 :question/id #uuid "984aecb3-dec8-597c-af46-aab2d57d3180" :question/math-academy-id "q-242921"} {:db/id 17592186180145 :question/id #uuid $$
(4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8).

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}

For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead make the expression under the square root positive or zero. 

For example, the domain of $\sqrt{x}$ is $x \geq 0,$ or $x \in [0,\infty)$ in interval notation.

On the other hand, the domain of $\sqrt{-x}$ is given by

$$
-x \geq 0
$$

which simplifies to

$$
x \leq 0.
$$

Thus, the domain of $\sqrt{-x}$ is $x \in (-\infty, 0].$

As another example, the domain of $\sqrt{x-1}$ is given by

$$
x -1 \geq 0
$$

which simplifies to

$$
x \geq 1,
$$

or $x \in [1, \infty)$ in interval notation. 

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}$ is shown below.

![](images/cb/cbae5f645d7774e114c483df27c8493c7e6a7f4fcf807ac7a14c54e4afa62105.png)

In general, to find the domain of a radical function of the form $y = \sqrt{g(x)},$ we need to solve the inequality $g(x) \geq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "149ca930-55b2-5261-97a0-91c331aecf92" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "12034629-2e9d-5e9e-9428-382566508681" :step/math-academy-id 21142 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125450}} {:db/id 17592186125450 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124548 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124357 :question/id #uuid "1a085da3-d8eb-52eb-94ea-4969fb74a83f" :question/math-academy-id "e-5876"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f00311f-e61b-5845-b19b-59cfbdb5871a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049072} {:db/id 17592186049799}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125125} {:db/id 17592186125151} {:db/id 17592186557232} {:db/id 17592186557288} {:db/id 17592186557292} {:db/id 17592186557315}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain of a Transformed Square Root Function"} :step/id #uuid "00a42fa0-7cac-5722-a8c6-a9c77cbe1379" :step/math-academy-id 21143 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125451}} {:db/id 17592186125451 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125803 :tutorial/content "Now, let's examine the range of a transformed radical function. For example, what is the range of 

$$
f(x) = -3\sqrt{5x-2}+7?
$$

The range of $\sqrt x$ is

$$
\sqrt x \ge 0.
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. So, we have

$$
\sqrt{5x-2} \ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-3$ and then adding $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5x-2} & \ge 0 \\ -3\sqrt{5x-2} & \le 0 \\ -3\sqrt{5x-2}+7 & \le 7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x) \in (-\infty,7].$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

:tutorial/content "To find the roots of a transformed radical function, we must set the function expression equal to zero and solve for $x.$ 

For instance, what are the roots of $f(x) = \sqrt{2x+1} + 5?$

In this case, we set

$$
\sqrt{2x+1} + 5 = 0.
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2x+1}+5 & =0 \\ \sqrt{2x+1} & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

This equation does not have any solutions since its left-hand side is always nonnegative, while the right-hand side is negative.

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no roots." :tutorial/id #uuid "a0803789-82d9-5ffd-91db-c1d02974a064" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4810 :tutorial/title "The Roots of a Transformed Square Root Function"} :step/id #uuid "df14bf6d-23b8-5ed1-9e7b-0662c3ed3d6f" :step/math-academy-id 29854 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125507}}] :activity/title "Properties of Transformed Square Root Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124687} {:db/id 17592186125449 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125802 :tutorial/content "The domain of a radical function is limited to the set of $x$-values that make the expression under the square root positive or zero.

In this case, we set

$$
\sqrt{2x+1} + 5 = 0.
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2x+1}+5 & =0 \\ \sqrt{2x+1} & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

This equation does not have any solutions since its left-hand side is always nonnegative, while the right-hand side is negative.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z}+yz) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1)\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1){e}^{z}+y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(1,1,1)} & =2(1+1){e}^{1}+1 \\  & =4e+1\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy}-{y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz}) & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot y \\  & =2z{e}^{xy}-{y}^{3}{e}^{yz}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}{|}_{(0,-1,1)} & =2(1){e}^{(0)(-1)}-(-1)^{3}{e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =2+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186380957 :question/id #uuid "9414edde-aaa5-55fe-99cf-fcbd12cf83ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-132255"} {:db/id 17592186381917 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3})-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot 2x \\  & ={z}^{3}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1,2)} & ={2}^{3}-2(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) \\  & =8-2(1)(-1) \\  & =8+2 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436607 :question/id #uuid "45d0ef52-763b-56d4-b138-648452f050d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-132258"} {:db/id 17592186436610 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi )} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(-1-\pi \cdot 0)+(-1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381279 :question/id #uuid "3444068d-2f79-5306-813a-47bbdab330c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-159725"} {:db/id 17592186381286 :question/id #uuid differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-{x}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot 0-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,9)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,9) & =-\frac{2\cdot 1}{9-{1}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048707} {:db/id 17592186049332} {:db/id 17592186050271} {:db/id 17592186050789} {:db/id 17592186051084} {:db/id 17592186193321 :question/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1) & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}(2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot (2x\cdot 1-0) \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{\sqrt{2xy-1}}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+1)^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1) & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (1+0) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381244 :question/id #uuid "4560fcbf-c2fb-5e9f-b888-53c870445e63" :question/math-academy-id "q-159655"} {:db/id 17592186381251 :question/id #uuid "We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1 \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-1,1)} & =3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+(1){e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =3+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436604 :question/id #uuid "0d55bb11-970c-5f1f-831a-44fb97e659c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132261"} {:db/id 17592186436608 :question/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186193890 :tutorial/content "We can use the chain, product, and quotient rules to find partial derivatives of multivariable functions. 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
f(x,y) = \cos(xy^2) + 3x
$$

To compute the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x,$ we "fix" the variable ${\color{blue}y}$ (in other words, we treat ${\color{blue}y}$ as if it were constant). Then, we take the derivative with respect to $x,$ as usual.

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2})+3x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2}))+\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2}))+\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+3\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot 1+3\cdot 1 \\  & =3-{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y,$ we "fix" the variable ${\color{blue}x}$ (in other words, we treat ${\color{blue}x}$ as if it were constant). Then, we take the derivative with respect to $y,$ as usual.

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2})+3x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2}))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x{y}^{2}))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})+0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot x\cdot 2y \\  & =-2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "66f2199e-b3f8-5590-80f3-bbac79027096" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6937 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c3b7bd9a-f6d4-521a-ab11-4ff2cecfbe07" :step/math-academy-id 41989 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193671}} {:db/id 17592186193680 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192794 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192518 :question/id #uuid "6f7bdbcf-fb8e-5c70-b368-4e73cc94bdb2" :question/math-academy-id "e-11112"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "35c6e3db-073b-5867-8137-1d8660b20887" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048842}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193183} {:db/id 17592186193190} {:db/id 17592186278246} {:db/id 17592186278247} {:db/id 17592186278248} {:db/id 17592186278249} {:db/id 17592186278251} {:db/id 17592186381258} {:db/id 17592186381265} {:db/id 17592186381272} {:db/id 17592186436605} {:db/id 17592186436606} {:db/id 17592186436613} {:db/id 17592186436614}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Quotient Rule"} :step/id #uuid "4bae0aea-9643-5e83-9379-45ac0682c9ca" :step/math-academy-id 42238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193698}} {:db/id 17592186193698 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193907 :tutorial/content "We can also compute partial derivatives of functions with three or even more variables.

$$

$$

Calculate the double integral

$$
\displaystyle\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A,

where $f$ is a function such that $m_{ij} = M_{ij} = 3$ for all partitions $P$ of $R,$ and $m_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion $R_{ij}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R,$ where the lower and upper sums respectively are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

and $m_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ in each subregion $R_{ij}.$ 

Now, since $m_{ij}=M_{ij}=3,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)=U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3({\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i})({\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}) \\  & =3(4-(-1))(2-1) \\  & =3\cdot 5\cdot 1 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)=15 & \le {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A\le 15=U(f,P),\end{aligned}
$$

which implies that

$$
\iint\limits_R f(x,y)\,\textrm d A = 15.

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $R=[-5,-2]\times [3,7]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$

Calculate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $f$ is a function such that ${m}_{ij}={M}_{ij}=1$ for all partitions $P$ of $R,$ and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P),
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R,$ where the lower and upper sums respectively are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

Now, since ${m}_{ij}={M}_{ij}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)=U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}1\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =({\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i})({\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}) \\  & =(-2-(-5))(7-3) \\  & =3\cdot 4 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
L(f,P)=12\le {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A\le 12=U(f,P)
$$

which implies that

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=12.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259570 :question/id #uuid "198f001c-8f0a-5ac7-9854-7515cac5441b" :question/math-academy-id "q-123846"} {:db/id 17592186341844 :question/id #uuid of X and Y"}] :question/problem "Let $R = [0,2]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+2{y}_{j-1})\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},\, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i}+2{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute $\displaystyle\iint\limits_R f(x,y)\,\textrm d A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\left(x_{i-1} + x_i\right)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j = (x_m^2 - x_0^2)(y_n-y_0)
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that $\bar{x}_i = \dfrac 1 2 (x_{i-1}+x_i)$ will always lie between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i,$ and similarly $\bar{y}_j = \dfrac 1 2 (y_{j-1}+y_j)$ will always lie between $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j.$ Therefore,

$$
x_{i-1} + {\color{blue}2}y_{j-1} \leq \dfrac{1}{2}(x_{i-1} + x_i) + {\color{blue}2}\cdot \dfrac 1 2 (y_{j-1} + y_j) \leq x_{i} + {\color{blue}2}y_{j},
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
x_{i-1} + 2y_{j-1} \leq \dfrac{1}{2}(x_{i-1} + x_i) + (y_{j-1} + y_j)\leq x_{i} + 2y_{j}.
$$

Multiplying this by $\Delta x_i\Delta y_j$ and applying the double summation gives

$$
L(f,P) \leq \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\left[\dfrac{1}{2}(x_{i-1} + x_i) + (y_{j-1} + y_j)\right]\Delta x_i \Delta y_j\leq U(f,P).
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P) \leq \dfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\left(x_{i-1} + x_i\right)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j + \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\left(y_{j-1} + y_j\right)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j\leq U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})(3-1)=4 \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(2-0)=16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 4+16\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 20\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
\iint\limits_R f(x,y)\,\textrm d A = 20.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129853 :question/id #uuid "08870289-b60b-524f-b96e-8c75f1f41bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-72627"} {:db/id 17592186129854 :question/id #uuid "186fcf52-8571-5f00-9ea4-41ddd0233cec" :question/math-academy-id "q-72908" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129220 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0b9d2e98-8007-51ec-bfb6-cb9b48029a2a" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Double Integral Using the Mean Value of X and Y"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93ad7135-7af4-5815-8cf3-b477ba14e4fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-42" :db/id 17592186128606} {:answer/id #uuid "e9d17dbb-b842-5e86-93b6-b94abf6d926c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-30" :db/id 17592186128607} {:answer/id #uuid "f50b36ff-4b31-5e69-bdc9-4343e8a58470" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-72" :db/id 17592186128608} {:answer/id #uuid "35aa6ea7-76f9-5ea5-9b70-b3444990b21d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-96" :db/id 17592186128609} {:answer/id #uuid "6de1f952-e217-513f-8bf6-7308d1a47ee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-84" :db/id 17592186128610}] :answer-field/id #uuid "458ba928-9cf2-59a6-b82f-e0f0a048274e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186128605}] :question/problem "Let $R = [2, 5] \cdot [- 2, 2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x, y)$ be a function defined over $R$.

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $R=[-3,1]\times [2,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
{y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i}\le \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})\le {y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{j-1}+{x}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-(-3)^{2})(4-2)=-8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})(1-(-3))=24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 24-(-8)\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 32\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=32.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544863 :question/id #uuid "ac9755ca-22ae-5d63-a731-5137b2daeebf" :question/math-academy-id "q-123850" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129220 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0b9d2e98-8007-51ec-bfb6-cb9b48029a2a" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Double Integral Using the Mean Value of X and Y"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "309eed89-dce7-588a-b072-9c591d942b77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186544194} {:answer/id #uuid "619565ed-3d57-5036-95fa-ba9547f31f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186544299} {:answer/id #uuid "8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186544402} {:answer/id #uuid "99233c84-4925-5f97-8b2b-7a305a74c813" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186544421} {:answer/id #uuid "cab1b35e-19f6-572c-9e9a-2c6be63ba9dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186544517}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186544402} :answer-field/id #uuid "01076285-ae72-5758-9587-05c045ac247c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186544649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $R=[0,2]\times [2,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0}) \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}-{x}_{0})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})(3-2)=4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({3}^{2}-{2}^{2})(2-0)=5 \\ 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =8(2-0)(3-2)=16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 16-4-5\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 7\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=7.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129221 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129040 :question/id #uuid "e75f2d8e-c165-5a24-942b-7326d7f11f0f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9497"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "89023510-57f4-52f9-90ed-eae07f48f707" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049348} {:db/id 17592186050883}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129422 :question/id #uuid "157470f8-e24e-5ffe-9569-91b340dbb848" :question/math-academy-id "q-123489"} {:db/id 17592186129423 :question/id #uuid "d2fe7b45-b659-56e0-83bf-d42ccd4288ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-123746"} {:db/id 17592186259547 :question/id #uuid "4c92a16d-8ec0-5bb7-a1d3-67db8dee714c" :question/math-academy-id "q-123737"} {:db/id 17592186259548 :question/id #uuid "013aa87f-4dba-5dcd-99b5-80fa5d543721" :question/math-academy-id "q-123740"} {:db/id 17592186259549 :question/id #uuid "8df0d876-87f5-5ec6-b4ea-583e00a0fa95" :question/math-academy-id "q-123741"} {:db/id 17592186259550 :question/id #uuid "2de9d676-815f-5c88-935f-91c621a59e79" :question/math-academy-id "q-123742"} {:db/id 17592186544824 :question/id #uuid "60f150de-1cdb-534e-a48d-461dca7bdb52" :question/math-academy-id "q-123747"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Definition of the Double Integral in Terms of Lower and Upper Riemann Sums"} {:db/id 17592186129040 :question/id #uuid "e75f2d8e-c165-5a24-942b-7326d7f11f0f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9497" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129221 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "89023510-57f4-52f9-90ed-eae07f48f707" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Definition of the Double Integral in Terms of Lower and Upper Riemann Sums"}] :question/problem "Let $R = [0,1]\times [1,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y) = 12-x-y.$ Further, let 

$$
\displaystyle I = \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y)\,\textrm dA
$$

be the unique number such that over all rectangular partitions $P$ of $R,$ we have 
$L(f,P)\:\leq I \:\leq U(f,P),$
where $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)$ are the corresponding lower and upper Riemann sums. Write down the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R,$ where the lower and upper sums respectively are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

and $m_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion $R_{ij}.$ 

We need to compute $U(f,P).$ 

Notice that for all subregions $R_{ij},$ we have that

- $f(x,y) = 12-x-y$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y) = 12-x-y$ decreases as $y$ increases.

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion. Therefore,

$$
M_{ij} = f(x_{i-1}, y_{j-1}) = 12-x_{i-1}-y_{j-1}
$$

and the upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
U(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (12-x_{i-1}-y_{j-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050883} {:db/id 17592186129422 :question/id #uuid "157470f8-e24e-5ffe-9569-91b340dbb848" :question/math-academy-id "q-123489"} {:db/id 17592186129423 :question/id #uuid and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$

$$
{m}_{ij}=f({x}_{i-1},{y}_{j})={x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j}+2

$$
L(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j}+2)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.

on a closed and bounded rectangle $R,$ and let $P = P_1\times P_2$ be a partition of $R.$ We know that the volume $V$ bounded by the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the region $R$ in the $xy$-plane satisfies

$$
L(f,P) \leq V \leq U(f,P),
$$

where $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$ are the lower and upper Riemann sums of $f$ with respect to $P.$

Imagine that our initial partition $P$ consists of a few rectangles only. Let's visualize the corresponding lower and upper Riemann sums, as shown below:

![](images/89/89ad0fd33f34cfad4f55fc2085360878460df92479f5f938ecd254420457f3f4.png)

 

Then, we refine $P$ by adding more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ resulting in more rectangles in $P{:}$ 

![](images/56/5635f58e19c47d6a9cfeab49c298ce5ca7aa1d8697e1b53390bb3bc31859637c.png)

 

Refining the partition once again, we get the following:

![](images/b2/b22f267ecf28627404eb90928e44d59b2873e88adc22ffaaa0a1a3335fffa307.png)

 

As we continue to refine $P$ by adding more and more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ we find that the values of the lower and upper Riemann sums approach the volume $V{:}$

- $L(f, P)\to V$ from below, and

- $U(f, P) \to V$ from above.

We define the **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ that satisfies the inequality

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

for *all* partitions $P$ of $R,$ and we write

$$
I=\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \text{d}A.
$$

The double integral gives the exact volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and $R.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b9ba8fdf-255d-53c2-832a-34ed3374abb0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3884 :tutorial/title 17592186130417 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've defined the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ (if it exists) that satisfies the inequality

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

for *all* partitions $P$ of $R,$ and we write

$$
I=\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \text{d}A.
$$

We note the following:

- Up to now, we've assumed that $f(x,y)$ is continuous and $R$ is closed and bounded. Whenever this is the case, a unique number $I$ will always exist.

- For positive, continuous functions, the double integral gives the exact volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and $R.$

- More generally, the double integral gives a signed volume. If $f$ is negative everywhere on $R,$ then the double integral of $f$ over $R$ is negative. If $f$ is both positive and negative on $R,$ then the double integral gives the difference between the positive and negative unsigned volumes. This is similar to the case with definite integrals for single-valued functions.

- Finally, It's possible to use this definition with functions that are not continuous. If a function $f$ (not necessarily continuous) is defined over $R,$ we say that $f$ is **Riemann integrable** over $R$ if a unique number $I$ can be found that satisfies the above inequality. Many (though not all) non-continuous functions are Riemann integrable." :tutorial/id #uuid "b0889acb-60da-5e9c-9f1b-530b118b05f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5824 :tutorial/title "Final Remarks"} :step/id #uuid "3c30b46b-78e4-5a7f-bec5-89ef0019d000" :step/math-academy-id 35700}] :activity/title "Defining Double Integrals Using Lower and Upper Riemann Sums" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129337} {:db/id 17592186130040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130379 :tutorial/content "Let $f(x,y)$ be a positive, continuous function defined on a closed and bounded rectangle $R,$ and let $P = P_1\times P_2$ be a partition of $R.$ We know that the volume $V$ bounded by the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the region $R$ in the $xy$-plane satisfies

:step/id #uuid "5af32a1a-efb5-509d-a196-f411e5d46fc5" :step/math-academy-id 35550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130122}} {:db/id 17592186130379 :tutorial/content "Let $f(x,y)$ be a positive, continuous function defined on a closed and bounded rectangle $R,$ and let $P = P_1\times P_2$ be a partition of $R.$ We know that the volume $V$ bounded by the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the region $R$ in the $xy$-plane satisfies

$$
L(f,P) \leq V \leq U(f,P),
$$

where $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$ are the lower and upper Riemann sums of $f$ with respect to $P.$

Imagine that our initial partition $P$ consists of a few rectangles only. Let's visualize the corresponding lower and upper Riemann sums, as shown below:

![](images/89/89ad0fd33f34cfad4f55fc2085360878460df92479f5f938ecd254420457f3f4.png)

 

Then, we refine $P$ by adding more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ resulting in more rectangles in $P{:}$ 

![](images/56/5635f58e19c47d6a9cfeab49c298ce5ca7aa1d8697e1b53390bb3bc31859637c.png)

 

Refining the partition once again, we get the following:

![](images/b2/b22f267ecf28627404eb90928e44d59b2873e88adc22ffaaa0a1a3335fffa307.png)

 

As we continue to refine $P$ by adding more and more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ we find that the values of the lower and upper Riemann sums approach the volume $V{:}$

- $L(f, P)\to V$ from below, and

- $U(f, P) \to V$ from above.

We define the **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ that satisfies the inequality

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

for *all* partitions $P$ of $R,$ and we write

$$
I=\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \text{d}A.
$$

The double integral gives the exact volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and $R.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b9ba8fdf-255d-53c2-832a-34ed3374abb0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3884 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130121 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129221 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129040 :question/id #uuid "e75f2d8e-c165-5a24-942b-7326d7f11f0f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9497"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "89023510-57f4-52f9-90ed-eae07f48f707" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049348} {:db/id 17592186050883}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129422} {:db/id 17592186129423} {:db/id 17592186259547} {:db/id 17592186259548} {:db/id 17592186259549} {:db/id 17592186259550} {:db/id 17592186544824}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Definition of the Double Integral in Terms of Lower and Upper Riemann Sums"} :step/id #uuid "38972544-74f5-555d-aadd-8581d0da7887" :step/math-academy-id 35559 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130039}} {:db/id 17592186130122 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130417 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've defined the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ (if it exists) that satisfies the inequality

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

for *all* partitions $P$ of $R,$ and we write

$$
I=\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \text{d}A.
$$

We note the following:

- Up to now, we've assumed that $f(x,y)$ is continuous and $R$ is closed and bounded. Whenever this is the case, a unique number $I$ will always exist.

- For positive, continuous functions, the double integral gives the exact volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and $R.$

- More generally, the double integral gives a signed volume. If $f$ is negative everywhere on $R,$ then the double integral of $f$ over $R$ is negative. If $f$ is both positive and negative on $R,$ then the double integral gives the difference between the positive and negative unsigned volumes. This is similar to the case with definite integrals for single-valued functions.

- Finally, It's possible to use this definition with functions that are not continuous. If a function $f$ (not necessarily continuous) is defined over $R,$ we say that $f$ is **Riemann integrable** over $R$ if a unique number $I$ can be found that satisfies the above inequality. Many (though not all) non-continuous functions are Riemann integrable." :tutorial/id #uuid "b0889acb-60da-5e9c-9f1b-530b118b05f9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5824 :tutorial/title "Final Remarks"} :step/id #uuid "3c30b46b-78e4-5a7f-bec5-89ef0019d000" :step/math-academy-id 35700} {:db/id 17592186130417 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've defined the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ (if it exists) that satisfies the inequality

$f(x)=5{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-x+12,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm 6, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that none of these potential roots are duplicates. Listing those potential roots in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm \frac{2}{5},\,\pm \frac{3}{5},\,\pm \frac{4}{5},\,\pm 1\,\pm \frac{6}{5},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{12}{5},\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 12.
$$

This makes a total of $24$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 12=24.$)"} {:db/id 17592186233825 :question/id #uuid "9a390fe0-f24c-5017-aa97-c03e1eb7dce0" :question/math-academy-id "q-321647"} has one of its roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-25$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-25}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 25,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{5}{3},\,\pm \frac{25}{3}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ are $-1$ and $-\frac{5}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{5}{3}$ | $3$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $25$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-15$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{5}{3},-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{5}{3}-\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186083682 :question/id #uuid "e7bd90fd-0fb1-553e-84d3-ad65f76b3093" :question/math-academy-id "q-39038"} {:db/id 17592186233828 :question/id #uuid distinct real roots of $f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $8$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }8}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ are $-4$ and $-2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $12$ | $-8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+4)({x}^{2}-3x+2) \\  & =(x+4)(x-1)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-4,1,2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-4+1+2=-1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186247321 :question/id #uuid "617dc73e-e9d7-5bc2-a43f-31dc7d4b171b" :question/math-academy-id "q-112984"} {:db/id 17592186247322 :question/id #uuid "5ec4e979-d834-5890-b36a-49ae78aa8863" :question/math-academy-id "q-112989"} {:db/id 17592186292903 :question/id #uuid "b8223b93-0903-5dfa-b5c3-229320695042" :question/math-academy-id "q-275954"} {:db/id 17592186302144 :question/id #uuid "44f388d6-5078-5e1a-a0fb-9aeba444134a" :question/math-academy-id "q-323610"} {:db/id 17592186302145 :question/id #uuid "3518da80-0db9-569e-b980-2b5efc57c5f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-323819" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "290c0af0-b447-58fd-8761-71af3c0f95df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186300157}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300157} :answer-field/id #uuid "3ea9a655-49ca-533c-8cb7-421e176fbf73" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186301433} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "060cda53-8668-5be5-8aef-25b100d05754" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186299961}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186299961} :answer-field/id #uuid "80e37fe1-bd7c-51e8-ba48-a531ae7460a1" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186301635} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b6ea38-f33a-5329-8a75-bcbcd85f7f0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186300028}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300028} :answer-field/id #uuid "b7f8d121-1dd4-5d54-b226-07216b17964f" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186301828}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The polynomial $f(x)=3{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}-9x-21$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-3,-2).$ In **ascending order**, the distinct real roots of $f(x)$ are

$$

$$

757} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084136 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084456 :tutorial/content "The **rational roots theorem** (or **rational zeros theorem**) describes the rational roots of a polynomial with integer coefficients. The statement of the theorem is as follows:

*Suppose that the rational number $\dfrac{{\color{blue}{p}}}{\color{red}{q}},$ in lowest terms, is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients. Then $\color{blue}p$ must be a factor of the polynomial's constant term, and $\color{red}q$ must be a factor of its leading coefficient.*

In other words, given a polynomial with integer coefficients, any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(x) = {\color{red}{8}}x^3+12x^2+6x+{\color{blue}{2}}.
$$

According to the rational roots theorem, any rational root of $f(x)$ must have a numerator that is a factor of $\color{blue}{2}$ (that is, either $\color{blue} \pm1$ or $\color{blue} \pm2$) and a denominator that's a factor of $\color{red} 8$ (${\color{red} \pm1},$ ${\color{red} \pm2},$ ${\color{red} \pm4},$ or $\color{red} \pm8$). 

At first glance, it may seem like we have $16$ possible rational roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{8}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{2}, & \pm \frac{2}{4}, & \pm \frac{2}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

However, if we reduce the above fractions to lowest form, we see that there are some duplicates, which we cancel out:

![](images/91/91d3a123202f03ecec2d568548b5964fdc941e77d9edbad8ab386954bb046740.svg) 

Removing the duplicates, we have ten *possible* rational roots. We list them from least to greatest in absolute value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{8}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm 1, & \pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Watch out!** The above roots are only *possible* rational roots. They are *not* guaranteed to be roots of our polynomial $f(x).$ The only guarantee is that if $f(x)$ has any roots that are rational numbers, they are included in the list of numbers above. Here, it turns out that the only actual root among the possibilities is $-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "85dfd162-8cfc-59dd-8f7d-d66bbde1873c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3729 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} $$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-25$ and the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-25}{\text{factor of }3}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 25,\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{5}{3},\,\pm \frac{25}{3}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-2,-\frac{1}{2}),$ are $-1$ and $-\frac{5}{3}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{5}{3}$ | $3$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-25$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $0$ | $25$ |
|  | $3$ | $0$ | $-15$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x+\frac{5}{3})$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+\frac{5}{3})(3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3(x+\frac{5}{3})(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5})\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{5}{3},-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{5}{3}-\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}.

$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-15$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }15}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 15.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(1,4)$ is $3.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-15$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $6$ | $15$ |
|  | $1$ | $2$ | $5$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-3)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-3)({x}^{2}+2x+5).
$$

Now we must see if the polynomial $g(x)={x}^{2}+2x+5$ has real roots. For this, we must find the value of its discriminant $D.$ Note that

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={2}^{2}-4(1)(5) \\  & =4-20 \\  & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D<0,$ the polynomial $g(x)$ doesn't have real roots.

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$

In this lesson, we will learn how to write down an expression for the upper Riemann sum for an *arbitrary* rectangular partition. 

As a concrete example, let $R = [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and define the function $f(x,y)$ as 

$$
f(x,y) = x^2+y^2.
$$

Further, let $P$ be an arbitrary partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our goal is to find an expression for $U(f, P),$ the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition. We proceed identically to the case where $P$ was fixed.

First, we consider an arbitrary subregion $R_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ over the $x$-axis and $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Since we're computing the *upper* sum, we're interested in the *maximum* value of $f$ in this subregion.

Notice that

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $x$ increases on $[0,1],$ and

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $y$ increases on $[0,1].$

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

Therefore, the *maximum* value of $f$ in the subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value of $f$ at the *top right corner* of the subregion.

![](images/6e/6e58954fccd74eaf67c95df818c4c9050c35b324c5fffe4902a366cb295b8845.png)

So, if $M_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ in each subregion, we have

$$
M_{ij} = f(x_{i}, y_{j}) = x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2
$$

for all $1\leq i\leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n.$
